title: Flowers that fade
hook: a traditional offering verse: these flowers fade, and so will this body

segments.voice: Yesterday, three bows: one for the Buddha, one for the dhamma, one for the sangha, pride set down on the floor. Your line was bow. What did the stiffness say? Day one hundred forty-one.

Most of the flowers we give are meant to say forever. Roses on an anniversary. A bouquet at a wedding. Plastic flowers, even, so they never droop. We choose the freshest ones, and when they start to brown we throw them out quickly, a little embarrassed, as if the flowers had failed us. Buddhist temples are full of flowers too: jasmine, lotus, frangipani, marigolds, heaped in front of the Buddha. But there's a verse people chant while offering them, and it says something you'd never write on a card.
screen: `ROSES THAT SAY FOREVER.` → `WE THROW THEM OUT, EMBARRASSED.` → `A VERSE YOU'D NEVER WRITE ON A CARD.`

segments.voice: The Theravada flower offering is a short Pali chant. It begins with the flowers themselves: full of color, full of fragrance, offered at the feet of the Buddha. Then it turns. In substance it says: just as these flowers will wither, so my body will go to destruction. Imagine saying that while holding a fresh bunch of jasmine. It's not meant to be gloomy, though, and many people who chant it say it doesn't feel gloomy. It's honest. The flowers are chosen precisely because they're fresh, and precisely because they won't last. That's the lesson: anicca, impermanence. Everything that arises passes away. The flower shows it in a few days. The body shows it over a lifetime. The Dhammapada uses flowers the same way. In Max Muller's translation: "Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers, and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village." The picture is someone so busy picking pleasures that they don't notice the water rising. The offering reverses that. You pick a flower, and you notice. What does noticing do? Teachers point out that it makes things more precious, not less. When you know the jasmine will be brown by Thursday, you smell it today. When you remember the people you love won't be here forever, you look at them longer at dinner. So the verse isn't asking you to be sad about fading. It's asking you to be awake while the flower is fresh. Buddhists offer flowers as respect for the Buddha, and they offer them as a mirror. The flowers are fresh today. That is exactly why they're beautiful.
screen: `COLOR, FRAGRANCE, AT HIS FEET.` · `AS THESE FADE, SO WILL THIS BODY.` · `ANICCA: EVERYTHING PASSES.` · `THE FLOOD AND THE SLEEPING VILLAGE.` · then, large: `FRESH TODAY, GONE TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: If you have a flower, a leaf, or even a picture of one, hold it or set it in front of you. Look at it closely for a few breaths: the color, the edges, where it's already starting to change. Then feel your own hands, warm, alive, also changing. There's nothing to fix. Let the breath come and go, each one arising and passing, fresh and then gone. Rest in that, gently. The bell holds the time.
Flowers that fade. The offering verse: as these flowers will wither, so will this body, and so this moment is worth waking up for.
Your line: fresh today, gone tomorrow. Today, offer one flower, at a shrine, on a table, to a person, and let it fade without throwing it out too soon. Day one hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists offer fresh flowers at shrines and temples while chanting a short Pali verse that reflects that, as the flowers wither, so will the body.

fork.setup: you're at a temple with a bunch of fresh jasmine. what do many Buddhists say while offering it?
options: as these flowers wither, so will this body.
fork.reveal: the Pali offering verse turns from the flowers' beauty to impermanence: as they fade, so will the body.

original.note: Pali: flower; the flower offering is puppha-puja.

trapdoor: what you thought: flowers are a pretty decoration for the Buddha.
what it means: a gift of respect and a mirror: as the flowers fade, so will the body.
what a scholar hears: the Pali verse runs 'puppham milayati yatha idam me, kayo tatha yati vinasabhavam': as this flower withers, so the body goes to destruction.

notes: The offering verse is paraphrased; the Pali line in the trapdoor ('Puppham milayati yatha idam me, kayo tatha yati vinasabhavam') should be checked against a standard chanting book.
Please check Max Muller's wording of Dhammapada 47 as quoted.
Flower types named (jasmine, lotus, frangipani, marigold) are illustrative.
Reviewer change: 'people who chant it don't find it gloomy' softened to 'many people who chant it say it doesn't feel gloomy', since it generalized about every practitioner.
